newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-NAGANO KNOWS IT CAN'T COUNT ON THE WEATHER.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NAGANO KNOWS IT CAN'T COUNT ON THE WEATHER.

text.p: Organisers of the 1998 Winter Olympic Games have been served notice not to count on the weather.
In a chilling reminder that 'Man proposes and the Weather disposes', all four pre-Olympic events held here have either been disrupted or ruined by too much snow or too little of it.
"Its the fate of the Winter Olympics," said Makato Kobayashi, director general of the Nagano Olympic Organizing Committee (NAOC). "We can't control the weather."
Heavy snow forced cancellation of two men's World Cup downhill races in Hakuba last March.
Then last month strong winds and heavy snows interfered with ski jumping and Nordic combined World Cup events.
Ski jumping officials called off competition on the normal hill on January 25 and only managed to hold the large hill event the following day after a four-hour postponement.
Competitors in the Nordic combined faced a 90-minute delay before the team jumping competition on January 30.
Earlier in January, lack of snow was the problem.
A last-minute snowfall saved a World Cup cross-country skiing competition after Japanese self-defence forces and hundreds of volunteers spent two days hauling snow to a near-barren course.
The only good omen for the organisers in the disruptions was that none of the four events were scheduled for the 16-day period in which the Games will be held next year.
The February 7-22 dates were chosen after consulting local weather patterns, Kobayashi said.
The fickleness of Nagano and its weather is due to cold Siberian winds that blow southward across the Sea of Japan towards Honshu, Japan's largest island.
Moisture picked up by the winds later falls as snow in the Nagano region, located in mountainous central Honshu.
Average February snowfall varies greatly among the Olympic venues, depending on topography and elevation.
Nagano, a city of 350,000 inhabitants located 360 metres (1,200 feet) above sea level and at the same latitude as San Francisco, receives a scant five cm (two inches).

Hakuba, site of the downhill, is at 700 metres (2,300 feet) and averages 59 cm (23 inches) with more than twice that amount falling at the top of the men's downhill course at 1,680 metres (5,500 feet).
A whopping 250 cm (100 inches) falls on 1,870-metre (6,130-foot) Mount Yakebitai, where Alpine events and snowboarding will be held.
Accurate weather forecasting in the mountainous, sea-influenced region is difficult, said Tamahiro Kimino, NAOC co-ordinator of weather information.
To help improve forecasting accuracy for the Olympics, a radar observatory was opened last November near Nagano.
Meteorologists collect information by sending out radio waves from the observatory, then measure strength and return speed of reflective waves after they strike rain or snow.

Previously, the mountains where many of the Olympic venues nestle were a blind spot for Japanese meteorologists who were forced to rely on large-scale satellite maps for weather-forecasting information.
